Except this view from Warsh, if correctly characterized, is just manifestly untrue. We know that the Fed announces the changes to short term interest rate. We can even argue that they determine/set it with independent agency to an extent in the short run. 

But it’s very hard to reject the hypothesis that the Fed reacts/follows to economic fundamentals rather than having the power to independently determine short interest rates to be a string of numbers whatever they want them to be. 

Presently, Warsh and indeed many other members of the FOMC would want nothing less than setting lower short interest rates forever. However, they are being forced to raise them by economic fundamentals: high inflation and low unemployment (fuel for sustained high inflation in the presence of supply cost shocks.).

How are Warsh & FOMC “forced” exactly? Through long term interest rates and term premiums. The fact of the matter is that the Fed *does not* determine the PATH OF SHORT TERM INTEREST RATES well into the future. They cannot possibly credibly commit to a path regardless of future economic fundamentals. And that’s the whole premise of “forward guidance” if people, incl Warsh himself, bothered to use it in its original intended meaning. 

If the Fed ignores fundamentals and set short rates too far away from what’s consistent with economic fundamentals for too long, say by keeping rates low despite inflation, buyers of long term bonds will balk and sell causing long term interest rates to rise, whatever the Fed’s plans for the path of short rates may be. The market will change its forecast of future short rates on behalf of the FOMC. And that’s before we talk about the concept of “term premium”. 

“Term premium” is an often derided academic concept, esp by non-academic financial watchers. TP = long-term rates - sum of expected short-term rates. Indeed, perhaps deservedly so bc it’s by nature quite pedantic and nearly impossible to measure well. This is bc “expectations” are nearly impossible to measure. Those that argue TP doesn’t exist may as well argue that expectations don’t exist bc they can’t be measured accurately, esp well into the future.

What’s the simplest/most intuitive scenario in which TP can arise? Suppose our collective mean expectations of short rates have not much changed, but our uncertainty over those mean expectations has risen a lot bc the world became much more uncertain. That increase in variance has to have a way to manifest in the long term bond prices: risk averse bond investors will demand higher bond yields/returns in exchange for bearing that risk of uncertainty

All of that is to say that I think Galbraith is wrong and as is often the “new economic thinking” stuff. It’s often some voodoo failing to understand basics. And I remain deeply unimpressed by the economic performance of the new Fed chair but also not surprised. 

He’s the man needed for the time just like Li Hongzhang was needed for the late Qing dynasty although with much less true skill/finesse and certainly displayed much less understanding. Li famously said towards the end of his life that he could only “paper over the cracks on the wall” rather than fixing the structural issues afflicting the Qing court.

If the objection was "don't steal results and attribute them properly" then I'd be the first to rush to agreement. I've been calling out & documenting the Navier-Stokes drama, so I'm with you there.

But that's mostly an OpenAI problem, not an AI solving math problems problem. Stealing results is a minor quibble in this letter, and is not the thrust of the objection.

From the letter:

The mathematical community functions, in many ways, as a miniature version of humanity. It consists of individuals using a wide variety of different approaches, joined by core values. The most precious resources of our profession are students and ideas, and these we nurture with great care. We feel responsible to let them grow to their full potential, until they can live a life of their own in the mathematical world. For students we often suggest problems with the core intention of developing skills making them well-positioned for advances in research and elsewhere. Our ideas we disseminate in talks, private discussions and careful writeups, connecting them to the previous ideas of others. These processes invariably take time and are based on human interaction.

In recent months, the success of AI in solving major mathematical problems has made headlines even outside mathematical circles. But solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight. Forgetting this in the world of AI may turn the tool against the primary goal. Indeed, the mass production at faster and faster pace of "true/false" statements could destroy fertile ground instead of breathing life into new ideas.

I've gone through a pretty insane dopamine detox over the last few months, and want to share some thoughts from the whole experience

The reason I wanted to do it was that my brain was utterly fried from the constant nonstop dopamine influx from social media, video games, junk food, netflix, email, and of course, the infinite online casino that is almost all of the crypto industry these days

It all felt incredibly unhealthy and unsustainable and while I didn't feel "unhappy", I did feel overwhelmed and like my brain was going to eventually explode if I kept going the way I was going

I'm not sure if it's just the way my brain works and if lots of people are able to adapt and run with this new world order we're finding ourselves in, or if this is some existential angst that is shared by most of the people reading this

But it really feels like things steamroll in one direction when it comes to dopamine and unless you're intentionally taking meaningful steps to protect yourself from the attacks, it's just gonna keep chipping away at your brain until you're forced to find some kind of reprieve

Personally, I stopped video games, deleted instagram and youtube from my phone, almost entirely stopped coming on X. I stopped watching TV, stopped scrolling feeds, stopped trading crypto, stopped sportsbetting or gambling.

The plan was to do it for 48-72hrs and then come back to reality, but that initial period was so blissful, I couldn't bring myself to come back.

Instead I stayed away. I checked in every now and then and kept up with some extremely basic work committments, and would occasionally watch a movie or something with the wife, but my screentime has basically been down 90%+ for the last 3 months

While a (big) part of me wishes I could stay like that forever, I also felt like I was missing something - the "productivity" lever of life. I had little projects I worked on, I played golf, I traveled, it was a utopian period really - anyone should be so lucky (and I am aware how lucky I am to have been able to take this time)

But it ultimately still left me feeling like I needed to come back to reality, to "work", to be a productive member of the world again - some way, some how

I'm not sure exactly what form that takes for me these days - I've tried so many things over the last couple of years, infinite pivots, and haven't quite found my lasting "thing" yet - if that's even a thing i'm gonna find. I've repeated some version of this cycle multiple times too - burnout, work hard, burnout, new idea, go hard, burnout, back to the memecoin trenches, burnout, launch new company, burnout, go all in on AI, burnout, burnout, burnout

I'm actually now sure what the point of this post is, now that I have gotten here. Maybe to tell everyone to take 2-3 days away from all the dopamine and rest your brains, see what it's like to live a life without technology for a bit

And that it is not "the answer". There is no "the answer" to any of this, we're all just rolling through life one day after another trying to figure it out, and no matter how utopian or good a certain lifestyle might seem, once you live it for a while, you'll usually find yourself wanting something else/different

Peace comes from within or something? Go figure, the monks had it right all along, and we all kinda know this deep down too - sometimes even explicitly - but sometimes we also need to be reminded of it again, and again, and again

David Friedberg: Frontier Models are Training on Your Novel Insights as “De-Identified Data”

@Jason:

“Should they trust any of these LLMs with their proprietary knowledge for fear of having it cribbed into a core LLM?”

@friedberg:

“I have had experiences where we've asked some fairly novel scientific questions, and (the AI model) identifies it as a novel insight.

It's like, ‘Oh, never thought about that, interesting, blah, blah, blah.’

And then using a different account, asking the next version (of the model) later, I've now experienced this.

It's like, ‘Oh, well, you could do this,’ and it actually just describes this exact thing that we had in our chat in the previous version.

Now, these are a handful of anecdotal experiences, but I know the domain that we work in, and the niche of it, and the ideation of this stuff, and the novelty of this stuff, and the lack of papers being published, and so on.

So I know that there isn't some new corpus of information out there that's training the new model.

So all I can say at that point is that my conversation or our analyses have been used for training.”

@DavidSacks:

“Okay, this does raise a really good question. What does it mean that the model is allowed to train on unidentifiable data?”

Friedberg:

“Well, that's my point. So it doesn't use any of my personal information, but it can use an insight derived from our chat, which it can then say is some training data that is unrelated.

But the truth is, it's actually a piece of IP that's our organization’s IP, and our engagement back and forth. We don't have any NDA or confidentiality provisions or protections with them being a service provider back to us.

This is why I care a lot about open source because I don't want them having my chat logs because they can use it for training to create an IP advantage that is now diffused to the rest of the market.”
